title.en: Quantization: How Do You Fit a Trillion-Parameter Model on a GPU?

description.en: This week's headline model ships at 2.4 trillion parameters. In bf16 that alone is a 4.8 TB download. Compute exactly how much smaller int8 and int4 weights make a model, and why quantization is what makes giant models servable at all.

story_variants.en:
## The Weights Have To Live Somewhere

"Every parameter in a model is a number, and every number needs bytes," Vaathiyaar says. "A model isn't just an idea — it's a file, and that file has a size. The bigger the model, the more that size starts to matter more than the model's cleverness."

### Bytes Per Parameter

Each weight is stored at some **precision**, and precision decides how many bytes one parameter costs:

> **model_bytes = num_params x bytes_per_param**

| Precision | Bytes/param |
|---|---|
| fp32 | 4 |
| bf16 / fp16 | 2 |
| int8 | 1 |
| int4 | 0.5 |

Going from bf16 to int8 doesn't shrink a model a little — it **halves** it. Going to int4 halves it again. That's not a rounding trick; it's storing each weight with fewer bits, which means less precision per number but far fewer total bytes.

### A Real Example

A 7B-parameter model in bf16 costs `7,000,000,000 x 2 / 1e9 = 14.0 GB` just for weights — before the KV cache you computed in `kv_cache_memory_footprint` even enters the picture. Quantize the same model to int8 and it drops to `7.0 GB`. Quantize to int4 and it's `3.5 GB` — a model that needed a datacenter GPU now fits on a laptop's.

### Why This Is In The News This Week

This week's big release, Qwen3.8-Max, ships at 2.4 trillion parameters. In bf16 that's `2.4e12 x 2 / 1e9 = 4,800 GB` — 4.8 **terabytes**, more memory than exists on any single GPU or even most multi-GPU nodes. In int4, it's `1,200 GB` — still huge, but the difference between 'needs a datacenter' and 'needs a rack' is exactly the quantization math you're about to implement.

> **Vaathiyaar's rule:** a model's parameter count tells you how smart it might be; its `bytes_per_param` tells you whether you can actually run it. Quantization is the lever that makes giant models deployable at all.

Today you implement the formula that turns a parameter count into a real memory bill, at any precision.

under_the_hood.summary: A model file is its parameter count times bytes per parameter, so storing weights in 8 or 4 bits instead of 16 halves or quarters the memory needed, which decides whether a model fits on a given GPU and how many GPUs a huge one needs.

steps.title: Bytes per parameter
steps.body: fp32 uses 4 bytes, bf16 or fp16 2, int8 1, and int4 half a byte. These are the only numbers needed to size a model's weights.

steps.title: Multiply
steps.body: quantized_size_gb(7e9, 2) = 14.0 GB; int8 gives 7.0 GB and int4 3.5 GB. Halving the bytes halves the whole model, which is why 4-bit versions fit consumer GPUs that cannot hold the bf16 original.

steps.title: Scale it up
steps.body: A one-trillion-parameter model needs 2 TB in bf16 and 0.5 TB in int4. On 80 GB GPUs that is at least 25 GPUs versus at least 7 just to hold the weights, before any KV cache.

output: 1e12 params x 2 bytes   = 2,000 GB -> >= 25 x 80 GB GPUs
1e12 params x 0.5 bytes = 500 GB   -> >= 7 x 80 GB GPUs

steps.title: Low-bit formats carry metadata
steps.body: Real 4-bit formats store a scale (and sometimes a zero-point) per group of weights, so the effective size is a bit above 4 bits per weight, for example around 4.5 with groups of 32 and 16-bit scales.

steps.title: What you trade
steps.body: Fewer bits mean rounding error in every weight. 8-bit is usually close to lossless for inference; 4-bit with good group-wise methods typically loses a little quality; below that, losses grow quickly. Always evaluate the quantized model on your task.

under_the_hood.takeaway: Model size is parameters times bytes. Quantization changes the bytes, and with them the hardware bill, at a measurable cost in accuracy.
